claim: BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact, case-sensitive match on the raw email, so a blocked address is bypassed by changing letter case (e.g. Bad@Spammers.org) or adding surrounding whitespace.
body:
## [ISSUE] Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and unnormalized, so blocks are trivially bypassed

**Severity:** HIGH — any blocked address can sign up by changing the case of one character.

### The Problem
```ruby
record = BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first
```
`email` is whatever `User.new_from_params` assigned (`user.email = params[:email]`, `app/models/user.rb:87`); nothing in `User` downcases or strips it before validation. The `blocked_emails.email` column is a plain `string` with a plain unique index (migration), and PostgreSQL `=` on `varchar` is case-sensitive.

### Theory / Proof
- The domain part of an address is case-insensitive per RFC 5321 section 2.4, and virtually every provider treats the local part case-insensitively too. `Bad@Spammers.org` and `bad@spammers.org` reach the same mailbox.
- The codebase already knows this: `Email.downcase` (`lib/email.rb`) and `User.find_by_username_or_email` normalise before lookup, and `User.email_hash` uses `email.strip.downcase`. The domain blacklist in `EmailValidator` uses a case-insensitive regex (`Regexp.new(..., true)`). The new per-address block is the only email check that is case-sensitive.

### What happens today vs. what will break
With `bad@spammers.org` blocked, signing up as `BAD@spammers.org` or `bad@Spammers.org` produces `WHERE email = 'BAD@spammers.org'`, finds no row, and the account is created. `match_count` is not incremented either, so the admin never sees the attempt.

### Research
Rails guides recommend normalising before persistence/lookup (`before_validation { self.email = email.downcase.strip }`); Devise does this by default via `config.case_insensitive_keys = [:email]` and `strip_whitespace_keys`.

### Recommendation
Normalise on both write and read:
```ruby
before_validation :set_defaults, :normalize_email

def normalize_email
  self.email = email.strip.downcase if email
end

def self.should_block?(email)
  record = BlockedEmail.where(email: email.to_s.strip.downcase).first
  ...
end
```
(or query `where('lower(email) = ?', email.strip.downcase)` backed by a `lower(email)` index).

claim: should_block? writes statistics as a side effect of validation, so match_count is inflated because UsersController#create validates twice (user.valid? then user.save), and the read-modify-write increment loses updates under concurrency.
body:
## [ISSUE] Statistics updated inside a validator are double-counted and racy

**Severity:** MEDIUM — the match statistics this PR introduces are unreliable.

### The Problem
```ruby
record.match_count += 1
record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now
record.save
```
This runs every time `EmailValidator#validate_each` runs. In `UsersController#create` (`app/controllers/users_controller.rb:167-171`) validation runs twice per request:
```ruby
if user.valid? && SiteSetting.call_discourse_hub?   # validation #1
...
if user.save                                        # validation #2
```

### Theory / Proof
- `user.valid?` runs outside any transaction, so its increment is committed.
- `user.save` (Rails 3.2 `ActiveRecord::Transactions#save` -> `with_transaction_returning_status`) runs validations inside a transaction. For an address with `action_type = do_nothing` the save succeeds and the second increment is also committed, so each signup counts **2**. For `block` the save fails and the second increment is rolled back, so it counts 1. The two action types therefore count differently for the same event.
- `match_count += 1` is a read-modify-write in Ruby: two concurrent requests both read N and both write N+1, losing an increment.

### What happens today vs. what will break
Admins who use `do_nothing` to "watch" an address see doubled counts; any other caller that calls `valid?` before `save` (a common pattern) inflates further.

### Research
Rails provides `update_counters` / `increment_counter` precisely to do atomic `SET x = x + 1` in SQL.

### Recommendation
Do the increment atomically and keep it out of the validation hot path where possible:
```ruby
def self.should_block?(email)
  record = BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first
  if record
    BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id)
                .update_all(["match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?", Time.zone.now])
  end
  record && record.action_type == actions[:block]
end
```
and in the controller replace the first `user.valid?` with a check that does not re-run the blocked-email lookup (or record the match once in the controller rather than in the validator).

claim: The domain regex @(domains) is not anchored at the end, so with a whitelist of example.com an address like x@example.com.evil.org passes the whitelist.
body:
## [ISSUE] Unanchored domain regex lets whitelist be bypassed with a suffix domain

**Severity:** MEDIUM — `email_domains_whitelist` does not actually restrict signups to the listed domains.

### The Problem
```ruby
domains = setting.gsub('.', '\.')
regexp = Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)
value =~ regexp
```
The pattern only requires `@example\.com` to appear somewhere; nothing anchors the end of the domain.

### Theory / Proof
With `email_domains_whitelist = "vaynermedia.com"`:
```ruby
"attacker@vaynermedia.com.evil.org" =~ /@(vaynermedia\.com)/i  # => 8 (match)
```
so the whitelist branch does not add an error, and anyone who controls `vaynermedia.com.evil.org` (or `vaynermedia.community`) can register. The blacklist has the mirror problem in the other direction only for subdomains (`x@sub.mailinator.com` is not matched since `@` must precede the domain).

### What happens today vs. what will break
This logic was moved verbatim from `User#email_in_restriction_setting?`, but it now lives in a reusable `EmailValidator` that the PR's intent ("comprehensive email validation") will spread to other models, so the flaw is worth fixing here.

### Research
Domain allow-lists conventionally match the full domain: `/@(#{domains})\z/i` (optionally allowing subdomains with `/@(.+\.)?(#{domains})\z/i`).

### Recommendation
```ruby
def email_in_restriction_setting?(setting, value)
  domains = setting.gsub('.', '\.')
  regexp = Regexp.new("@(#{domains})\\z", true)
  value =~ regexp
end
```
and add a spec: whitelist `vaynermedia.com` must reject `x@vaynermedia.com.evil.org`.

claim: rejectedEmails: Em.A([]) is defined on the class prototype in extend(), so the same array instance is shared by every CreateAccountController instance.
body:
## [ISSUE] `rejectedEmails` array is shared across controller instances

**Severity:** LOW — state leaks between instances; mostly latent because the controller is a singleton.

### The Problem
```js
rejectedEmails: Em.A([]),
```
Properties passed to `Ember.Object.extend` live on the prototype. Arrays/objects there are shared by reference across all instances, so `pushObject` on one instance mutates all of them.

### Theory / Proof
This is a documented Ember pitfall ("arrays and objects defined in extend are shared between instances; initialize them in `init`").

### What happens today vs. what will break
Today the container gives one controller instance, so behaviour is correct. Any test that creates multiple instances (`Discourse.CreateAccountController.create()`), or a future change to non-singleton controllers, will see rejected emails from one instance flagged in another.

### Recommendation
```js
init: function() {
  this._super();
  this.set('rejectedEmails', Em.A([]));
},
```
